newsitem.title: USA: Downgrade will not cost L.A. in near-term - official.
newsitem.headline: Downgrade will not cost L.A. in near-term - official.

text.p: The chief of debt administration for the city of Los Angeles said on Monday that last week's downgrade of city debt should not increase its borrowing costs in the near-term.
"There shouldn't be any cost impact on the city" because the city does not plan to issue general obligation bonds in the near-term, said Gerry Miller, the Los Angeles official.
On Friday, Moody's Investors Service Inc said it reviewed and lowered the rating on the city's general obligation bonds to Aa from Aa1.

Moody's said a primary reason for the rating downgrade was the reduction in revenue flexibility as a result of Proposition 218, which amended the state Constitution to require voter approval of most tax or fee increases and curtailed the use of many types of assessments.
"Their concern is understandable," Miller said. "They were concerned with (Proposition) 218 as well they should be."
Miller said, however, that Proposition 218 was not expected to have a large impact on the city's budget, at least not in the near-term.
"I don't think the impacts of 218 are really going to be felt until we're in another recession," Miller said.
Standard & Poor's Corp has told city officials that it was not planning to take any rating action against the city at this time, Miller said.
